prime.problem: A pretrained base model only continues text; you can't ship it. Turning it into a chat or reasoning model takes SFT, RL and sometimes distillation, and each stage hands something different to the serving team: new weights, a context length, and an output-length distribution that can make traffic far more decode-heavy.
prime.fits: Last training card. Builds on compute-budgets (post-training is tiny next to 6ND, except when it isn't) and the training-step memory count (a trained model costs 16 bytes/param, a frozen one 2). It hands off to the economics half: what serving receives.
expect: SFT: loss on the response tokens only
PPO's four models vs GRPO's group baseline
the RL rollout as an inference job
distillation: Hinton soft targets vs SFT on teacher samples
what serving receives: checkpoint, precision, context, output lengths
prime.goal: Compute a GRPO advantage by hand, explain why reasoning RL is mostly inference, and say what each post-training choice changes for the servers.

attend: Which of PPO's four models does GRPO delete, and what replaces it?
When all 16 answers in a group get the same reward, what does the update learn, and what did those rollouts cost?
Why does an RL step wait for its longest answer, and what does the GPU do meanwhile?
R1's "distillation" never shows the student a probability. What does it show instead, and what does that allow?
R1's RL cost 29× V3's post-training. Which part of the RL step grew?

must: PPO needs a value model to estimate reward-to-go per token → it's about policy-sized (another 128.5 GB for an 8B-sized policy, ours) and hard to train when reward comes only at the end → GRPO samples G answers per question and uses (r − mean)/std as the advantage → no critic, and all-equal groups give zero gradient

An RL step = rollout (generate) + score + one training update → at 8,192 answers per rollout and up to 65,536 tokens each, generation dominates → the step waits for its longest answer, decoding a tiny batch → RL for reasoning is an inference job with a training step attached, run on vLLM with MTP speculation

Reward rewards correct answers, not short ones → R1-Zero's response length rose through training → the served model writes thousands of thinking tokens (8,793 on hard math) → traffic becomes decode-heavy: KV held for thousands of steps, KV budget caps the batch, preemption gets expensive

Sequence-level SFT on 800k teacher samples → teacher runs once, no shared vocabulary needed → small dense students (1.5B–70B) that beat RL on the same small model (72.6 vs 47.0 AIME for 32B) → but inherit the teacher's long outputs, so $/answer = $/M × tokens per answer
elevated: GRPO's 16 answers share one prompt → prefix sharing (Llama 3's PagedAttention reuse gave over 2× in rejection sampling) and MTP self-speculation (1.8× decode) cut rollout time → every serving-side speedup shortens the RL bill

Hinton's temperature softmax and the T² gradient factor
the R1-Distill base models and learning rates (Table 6)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the pipeline pretrain → SFT → RL → distill → serve, and under each arrow write what it costs (rough GPU-hours for DeepSeek) and what it hands to inference. Then one sentence on why reasoning RL is mostly inference.
checklist: pretrain 2,664K + context 119K H800-hours → weights + context length; optimizer state dropped
RL: rollouts dominate; R1 147K, grows with answer length
distill: SFT on teacher samples → smaller model, still long outputs
serve: decode-heavy load, KV budget and TPOT matter

retrieve.q: Explain what the group baseline in GRPO replaces, and why that matters for memory and for long reasoning answers.
answer: it replaces PPO's learned value model (critic), which is about policy-sized
the advantage is how much better an answer did than its siblings on the same question
no critic to hold (289.1 → 160.6 GB for an 8B-sized setup, ours) and no per-token value to learn when reward arrives only at the end of a long chain

retrieve.q: Walk through one R1 RL step's four modules and say which are inference, which train, and what the step waits on.
answer: rollout: vLLM workers sample G answers per question (EP, redundant experts, MTP speculation)
inference: reward and reference models run a forward pass over every sample
rule-based reward: code execution and answer matching, async, on CPU
training: the only backward pass (packing, DualPipe)
it waits for the longest rollout to finish

retrieve.q: You need a cheap reasoning model for math at 8B scale. Compare serving R1, running RL on the 8B, and SFT on R1's samples.
answer: serve R1: best quality, ~671 GB FP8, at least a node per replica
RL on the small model: expensive and worse (Qwen2.5-32B: 47.0 vs 72.6 for the distilled 32B)
SFT on teacher samples: cheap, one H100 for an 8B student
but all three produce long outputs; if answers must be short, a non-reasoning model can be cheaper per request

retrieve.q: Compute the GRPO advantages for one question with G = 16 answers of which 4 are correct (reward 1) and 12 wrong, and check that they sum to zero.

compare.q: That card runs GRPO on a laptop for a coding agent; this one runs it at DeepSeek scale. What is identical in the mechanism, and which cost dominates at each scale?
answer: identical: sample a group, score each answer by execution or rules, advantage = reward relative to the group, no value model
identical failure: an all-equal group gives zero gradient
on a laptop, a few short answers: training and scoring are comparable
at R1 scale, up to 65,536-token answers: rollout generation dominates, so inference speed sets the RL bill

compare.q: A distilled reasoning model reaches your scheduler. What changes in its KV budget and preemption decisions compared with a chat model, and why?
answer: each request holds its KV for thousands of decode steps
KV per sequence grows large (8.59 GB at 65,536 tokens for an 8B-architecture student: 7 fit in 63.9 GB vs 238 at 2k)
so memory, not compute, caps the batch, and preempting a long request throws away a lot of work

predict.q: Halve the answer-length cap from 65,536 to 32,768 tokens for an 8B-sized policy on one H100 at the batch-1 floor. Does the time to write the longest answer halve? Commit, then check with the card's formula.
predict.answer: It more than halves. Time ≈ n·W/BW + KV·n(n−1)/2 ÷ BW; the second term grows with n², so 65,536 → 32,768 takes 398.2 s → 178.1 s (2.24× faster, our arithmetic). With MTP's 1.8×, 98.9 s. The quadratic KV-read term is why the tail of long answers dominates rollout time.

apply.task: (1) A GRPO group has G = 8 answers, 3 correct (reward 1) and 5 wrong (0). Compute the mean, the population std and every advantage, and check they sum to zero. (2) Now all 8 are correct. What is every advantage, and what did those 8 rollouts buy? (3) For an 8B-architecture student serving 32,768-token answers on one H100 (128 KiB of KV per token, 63.9 GB free after the weights), how much KV does one sequence hold, and how many fit?
apply.done: (1) mean 0.375, std 0.484, correct +1.29, wrong −0.775, and 3 × 1.29 − 5 × 0.775 ≈ 0. (2) Every advantage is 0 (std 0, guarded), so the group produces no gradient: 8 generations for nothing. (3) 4.29 GB per sequence, 14 sequences, against 238 at 2k context.
apply.hint: std = √(p(1 − p)) for 0/1 rewards with p = share correct.
